item.title: China-India border situation 'remains generally stable'; expert says dialogue a shared understanding to help prevent escalation of friction
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 21:50:00
Chen Xi, spokesperson for China's Ministry of National Defense The situation in the China-India border areas remains generally stable, a Chinese Ministry of National Defense spokesperson said at a press conference on Thursday. Chen Xi, spokesperson for the ministry, stressed that the Zangnan region is China's territory and that China does not recognize the so-called "Arunachal Pradesh" illegally set up by India. China and India maintain communication through diplomatic and military channels, including general-level talks, to jointly implement the consensus reached by the two sides and safeguard peace and tranquility in the border areas. He made the remarks when asked about reports that Chinese and Indian military officials held high-level talks this month in the so-called "Arunachal Pradesh" (China's Zangnan), with border management among the key topics. Chen's remarks came a day after the Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson said at a media briefing on Wednesday that a meeting of the senior military commanders was held in the eastern sector recently. Discussions between the two sides focused on improving border management as well as addressing outstanding issues along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the Indian Express reported. The ministry's spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that "India and China engage regularly through diplomatic and military mechanisms" when responding to questions. Jaiswal also said that such interactions are aimed at maintaining peace and tranquility in the border areas and preventing any escalation, per the Indian Express report. The recent statements by China and India on senior military commander-level talks in the eastern sector, coupled with China's reaffirmation of its sovereignty over Zangnan region, send a clear signal that China's position on territorial sovereignty remains firm, while maintaining stability through dialogue remains a shared understanding between the two sides, Qian Feng, director of the Research Department at Tsinghua University's National Strategy Institute, told the Global Times on Thursday. The two sides have continued to communicate through military and diplomatic channels to prevent local friction from escalating, using existing meeting mechanisms as a pressure valve to ease tensions, Qian said. China and India agreed at the 25th round of talks between their Special Representatives on the boundary question in Beijing on August 25 to strengthen border management mechanisms, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry. Strengthening border management mechanisms was among the outcomes of the 25th round of talks between the Special Representatives of China and India on the boundary question, held in Beijing on August 25. The two sides reached eight points of outcomes and consensus including agreements to address situations on the ground through existing diplomatic and military channels, resolve outstanding issues and avoid misunderstandings and miscalculations along the LAC. The two sides also agreed to add two meeting points for general-level talks and establish two additional border military hotlines in the eastern and middle sectors, according to the Chinese Foreign Ministry. On October 26, responding to Indian claims that Chinese forces had diverged from established patrolling patterns, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said China strictly abides by the relevant agreements and common understandings reached between the two countries, and conducts normal border patrol and control activities to safeguard its territorial sovereignty and stability in the border areas. China and India maintain communication through diplomatic and military channels. We hope that India will work with China in the same direction by jointly implementing the common understandings reached between the two sides and maintaining peace and tranquility in the border areas with concrete actions.

item.title: World's first Tibetan-language search engine marks 10th anniversary with 1.3 million daily visits on average
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 21:42:00
Tourists pose for photos at Potala Palace square in Lhasa, Southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on October 15, as the 2026 "Winter Tour in Xizang" campaign launches. From October 15, 2026 to March 15, 2027, all A-level scenic spots in Xizang (except temple sites) are open to visitors free of charge. Photo: CNS Photo Yongzin.com, the world's first Tibetan-language search engine, now records an average of 1.3 million visits per day as it marked its 10th launch anniversary. The search engine serves users across all 34 provincial-level regions in China and 96 countries and regions worldwide, including the US, France, Japan, Russia and Singapore, China News Service reported on Thursday. Serving as a unified gateway to major Tibetan-language websites across China, a major source of Tibetan-language information on the internet and a resource-sharing hub, yongzin.com has evolved into a comprehensive Tibetan-language online system built around information sharing and search services. The system integrates a Tibetan-language search engine, multi-platform applications, an automatic Tibetan word-segmentation and intelligent language analysis system, and a high-efficiency web crawler. Over the past decade, the platform has undergone continuous upgrades, addressing gaps in the supply of Tibetan-language online information while expanding its range of services. Initially offering searches for webpages, news, images, audio and video, it has gradually expanded to include a Tibetan-language encyclopedia, document library and question-and-answer system. It has also launched supporting products such as a mobile app and a Tibetan-Chinese (Putonghua)-English input tool, with total mobile downloads exceeding 3 million. At present, the platform's document library contains more than 90,000 volumes and articles of Tibetan ancient texts, academic literature and folk writings. Its collections cover more than 30 fields, including politics, economics, history, literature, Tibetan medicine and natural sciences. The recently launched version 3.0 of the search engine has undergone a complete overhaul of its underlying architecture. It introduces four new modules including Tibetan optical character recognition (OCR), bidirectional Chinese-Tibetan machine translation, Tibetan academic search and a Tibetan calligraphy section. It also integrates Tibetan-language voice search, with speech recognition accuracy exceeding 92 percent. In addition, the bidirectional Chinese-Tibetan machine translation module, powered by a large AI model, can accurately translate Chinese-language documents into Tibetan, making information more accessible to grass-roots rural and pastoral communities. The Tibetan academic search function overcomes the limitations of the previous version, which only supported title searches, by enabling advanced searches by author, keywords and full text, filling a gap in specialized Tibetan-language academic search services. The newly launched Tibetan calligraphy section also enriches the digital presentation of the Tibetan ethnic culture. According to the platform's development plan, the yongzin.com platform will complete the integration of its speech synthesis function by the end of this year, adding audio playback to help users access news reports and classical texts. Global Times

item.title: China's 2030 roadmap targets 6G, computing networks, 'paving way for new industries and growth models'
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 20:41:00
6G File Photo: VCG China unveiled a 2030 roadmap for building a next-generation communications network on Thursday, placing 6G, computing infrastructure, and advances in core technologies at the heart of its push toward an intelligent economy. The plan calls for launching commercial 6G services when appropriate and promoting breakthroughs in high-end chips and key software and their large-scale adoption. Jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), the Cyberspace Administration of China, and the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), the plan outlines the coordinated development of four types of networks - foundational, space-based, international, and integrated networks. It also calls for greater intelligence across networks, stronger security and resilience, and greener, lower-carbon operations, backed by a stronger industrial ecosystem and greater policy and resource support, with the aim of building on China's competitive strengths and leading position in the information and communications industry. The roadmap is part of a broader push to develop six major infrastructure networks during China's 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30). The MIIT described the new network as the "nervous system" of the economy and society, underpinning the digital and intelligent transformation of five other infrastructure networks covering water, next-generation power grids, computing, urban underground pipelines, and logistics. Chinese experts likened China's initiative to the US "information superhighway" plan of the 1990s, emphasizing its potential to reshape the economy. Just as the internet paved the way for e-commerce and the sharing economy, the new infrastructure could give rise to a new generation of industries and business models. China's advantage lies in its vast market and diverse industrial applications. Bringing communications, computing, and energy infrastructure into closer alignment could help turn these strengths into a more powerful engine for technological innovation and industrial upgrading, while opening up new avenues for international economic cooperation, experts said. Wiring the AI era The new network will be built around technologies such as 5G-Advanced (5G-A), 6G, 10-gigabit optical networks, and satellite internet, providing a broad range of information services, from sensing and data transmission to storage, computing, and intelligence, according to the plan. The MIIT identified four major advances over conventional communications networks: extending connectivity beyond people to machines, objects, and AI agents; expanding coverage across land, sea, air, and space; delivering higher access speeds, lower latency, and greater connection density; and integrating communications, sensing, navigation, computing, and intelligence. China has already built the world's largest information and communications network, with advanced technological capabilities. With communications technologies evolving rapidly, AI driving digital transformation, and network security challenges growing more complex, building the new infrastructure moderately ahead of demand will help China seize opportunities in digital industrial transformation and support high-quality economic and social development, the ministry said. "The initiative is essentially about building infrastructure suited to the needs of an intelligent economy," Liu Gang, chief economist of the Chinese Institute of New Generation Artificial Intelligence Development Strategies and director of the Institute of Economics at Nankai University, told the Global Times on Thursday. Traditional communications networks are designed primarily to transmit information. AI, however, requires a range of capabilities, from sensing, storage, and computing to analysis, decision-making, and execution, Liu said, adding that it places far greater demands on what networks can do and how they perform. "Technologies such as 6G and satellite internet could support a wide range of industrial applications, from autonomous driving and the low-altitude economy to intelligent manufacturing, helping drive China's industrial upgrading and structural improvements in the manufacturing sector," Liu noted. Sharing infrastructure across different services could generate economies of scale and lower the cost of industrial development, Hu Qimu, a professor at the Maritime Silk Road Institute of Huaqiao University, told the Global Times. "Functions that previously required several separate networks could be delivered through a single integrated network. Businesses can use the same infrastructure for communications, computing, and AI services, creating greater scope for industrial convergence and upgrading," Hu said. The plan also gives considerable weight to the development of computing infrastructure. It calls for supporting computing power providers in the orderly development of clusters with more than 10,000 accelerator cards, building 400Gbps and 800Gbps transmission links between computing hubs and areas with high demand, and introducing 1.6Tbps transmission systems on a trial basis. The country will also develop a multilevel computing infrastructure spanning hub, regional, and edge facilities, and establish a unified national platform to monitor and schedule computing resources, according to the plan. The emphasis on connectivity and coordinated resource allocation reflects the differing computing needs of AI applications, Liu said. Autonomous driving, for instance, requires nearby computing resources for real-time responses, while less time-sensitive data processing can draw on facilities in western China. Linking these resources would help meet growing demand from industry and scientific research more efficiently. Large-scale computing clusters, meanwhile, are particularly important for AI model training. Their development could spur wider adoption of domestically developed computing chips, improve hardware-software compatibility, and accelerate technological improvements, Liu noted. Innovation without borders Alongside its push to build infrastructure for an intelligent economy, China is placing greater emphasis on technological self-reliance and international cooperation. The roadmap aims to strengthen China's self-reliance and control over industrial and supply chains by 2030. It calls for breakthroughs in 6G, ultra-high-speed optical communications, and satellite communications, as well as closer collaboration across the chip, software, and communications equipment industries to accelerate the development and widespread adoption of high-end chips and key software. The roadmap also seeks to expand China's global digital connectivity by extending submarine cable links along Asia-Pacific and Asia-Europe routes, advancing the development of a BRICS submarine cable network, coordinating the overseas deployment of data centers and cloud infrastructure, and supporting the global expansion of computing services, AI models, and applications. The plans come amid growing US restrictions on access to key technologies. Recent measures include new controls on remote access to advanced AI chips and additional Entity List designations, while US lawmakers are weighing further restrictions on exports of chipmaking equipment to China. Developing homegrown technologies could help China overcome external restrictions, but the strategic gains extend further, Hu said. "Wider industrial adoption could enable China to develop business models suited to its industrial strengths and gain a greater voice in shaping international standards and industry rules." Efforts to shape international 6G standards are gathering pace across major economies. Industry groups in the US, Japan, and South Korea are working to coordinate their 6G technology roadmaps and identify common technical requirements, while the EU's 2026 ICT standardization plan seeks European leadership in setting global standards for key 6G technologies. However, diverging standards could drive up costs and limit interoperability across markets, undermining the economies of scale on which the global telecommunications industry relies, industry analysts said. China's roadmap, meanwhile, emphasizes international cooperation, calling for active participation in international standard-setting bodies such as the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and the 3rd Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), alongside further opening-up of value-added telecommunications services through pilot programs. Greater alignment on technical standards and industry rules could help reduce cross-border investment risks, Hu said. China's emphasis on international standards cooperation could also help prevent market fragmentation and create new opportunities for industrial cooperation in the digital economy.

item.title: China's super-large tunnel boring machine 'Jianghai' completes 7.46-km underwater crossing under Yangtze River
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 16:41:00
The section of the Haitai Yangtze River Tunnel that needs to be excavated using a tunnel boring machine in Suzhou, East China's Jiangsu Province. File photo: VCG China's domestically developed 16-meter-class super-large-diameter shield machine Jianghai finished a 7.46-kilometer underwater tunneling run beneath the Yangtze River on Thursday, after about 14 months of tunneling. This represents a milestone for the Haitai Yangtze River Tunnel, which is set to become the world's longest cross-river highway shield tunnel. The project is now entering the final phase of tunnel excavation. The successful river crossing validates China's capability to deploy and operate super-large-diameter shield equipment under some of the most complex underwater conditions. It also clears a critical path toward the timely overall breakthrough of what is expected to be the world's longest cross-river highway shield tunnel. As the project lies in the heart of the Yangtze River Delta, one of China's most economically dynamic regions, which includes Shanghai, the completion of the tunnel will significantly cut travel times among cities in the region and thus strengthen the "one-hour economic circle." The Jianghai tunnel boring machine (TBM), weighing more than 5,000 tons, began its drive in April 2025. Workers guided it through three demanding phases: steady entry into China's longest river, a long downhill advance to the deepest point - 75 meters below the riverbed - and an uphill climb with attitude adjustments to exit the water, according to China Railway 14th Bureau Group, the builder of the tunnel. Working conditions were extreme. The mixed soft-soil strata under the Yangtze River are highly permeable. At the lowest point, water and earth pressure reached 7.5 bar - equivalent to the weight of about 51 cars per square meter. Even minor deviations in the machine's posture risked water and sand inrushes or ground instability. Project teams relied on advanced digital monitoring, continuous 24-hour parameter tracking via a smart shield-control platform, atmospheric-pressure cutter changing, and other techniques to maintain millimeter-level control. The Haitai Yangtze River Tunnel links Haimen District in Nantong city on the north bank of the Yangtze with Taicang and Changshu on the south bank, both in East China's Jiangsu Province. An aerial view of the entrance of the Haitai Yangtze River Tunnel, in Nantong's Haimen District, East China's Jiangsu Province, on November 26, 2026 Photo: VCG The full route measures 39.07 kilometers and is being built to bidirectional six-lane expressway standards with a design speed of 100 kilometers per hour. The under-river section alone stretches 11.185 kilometers, with 9,315 meters being excavated using a TBM, according to media reports. The tunnel is expected to ease pressure on the existing Sutong (Suzhou-Nantong) Bridge across the Yangtze River, significantly cut travel times between Nantong and southern Jiangsu as well as Shanghai, and strengthen the "one-hour economic circle" of the Yangtze River Delta core area. Global Times

item.title: Think Asia Forum 2026 held in Singapore, focusing on regional cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 08:44:00
Zhu Guangyao, China's former vice finance minister, delivers a keynote speech in the Think Asia Forum 2026 in Singapore, on Nov. 25, 2026. The Think Asia Forum 2026 was held in Singapore on Wednesday, bringing together participants to discuss how openness, innovation and cooperation can drive Asia's development through collaboration in areas such as media, think tanks and local partnerships. (Xinhua/Then Chih Wey) The Think Asia Forum 2026 was held in Singapore on Wednesday, bringing together participants to discuss how openness, innovation and cooperation can drive Asia's development through collaboration in areas such as media, think tanks and local partnerships. Chinese Ambassador to Singapore Cao Zhongming said in his opening remarks that Asia's development should promote broad-based prosperity while addressing the needs of different countries and communities, ensuring that the benefits of growth are shared more widely across the region. China will work with other Asian countries to promote peace, strengthen cooperation, expand openness and foster greater inclusiveness across the region, he said. Yu Yunquan, vice president of the China International Communications Group, said the organization will draw on its strengths in people-to-people exchanges and think tank research to deepen cooperation among Asian think tanks. It will support exchanges and joint research among scholars, media professionals and young people from different countries, and help turn ideas into practical recommendations for regional development, he said. Yu called on countries to expand Asia's development opportunities through openness and cooperation, safeguard regional peace and stability through dialogue, and shape the region's future through intellectual exchange. Qiu Linchuan, chair of the Wee Kim Wee School of Communication and Information at Nanyang Technological University, said genuine openness means countries maintaining the autonomy to chart their own development paths, while ensuring that the flow of goods, capital, data and knowledge serves local communities. It also means listening to voices from the Global South and addressing the concerns of grassroots workers and rural communities, he said. Innovation, he said, should extend beyond cutting-edge technologies to include new approaches to institutions, governance and communication, while also drawing on local resources to promote inclusive growth and reduce inequality. Asian cooperation, Qiu added, should build on the region's longstanding traditions of interaction and begin with practical joint initiatives, such as think tanks sharing expertise and conducting joint research. Zhu Guangyao, China's former vice finance minister, said in a keynote speech that the world is at a critical juncture in the fourth industrial revolution, driven by artificial intelligence (AI), and that regulatory frameworks need to keep pace with technological advances. Asia has an important role to play in this process, Zhu said. He outlined three priorities for regional cooperation: avoiding taking sides and pursuing an independent development path for Asia, strengthening policy coordination and aligning rules, and developing blockchain infrastructure as shared public infrastructure for the region. Alfred Schipke, director of the East Asian Institute at the National University of Singapore, told Xinhua that Asia's large middle-class population and its contribution of about two-thirds of global economic growth reflect its significant potential, both for the region and the rest of the world. Asia has considerable opportunities in digital technology, AI, the development of the ASEAN Power Grid and investment, he said. The region's experience in the digital economy, particularly in payment systems, as well as its advances in AI, can also offer valuable lessons for other parts of the world, he added. Chong Sin Woon, former deputy education minister in Malaysia, said that cooperation in business, technology and trade ultimately depends on people-to-people exchanges, adding that youth exchanges and educational cooperation are key to strengthening Malaysia-China and China-ASEAN ties. More Chinese students have been studying in Malaysia in recent years, while more Malaysian students are choosing China over Western countries, creating new opportunities for educational cooperation in Asia, he noted. Huang Rihan, dean of the Maritime Silk Road Research Institute at Huaqiao University, said that Asian countries have their own strengths in industry and technology, and that building mutual trust is key to harnessing these complementary strengths for shared development. He said countries could foster greater understanding and trust through stronger policy dialogue between governments, closer networks among universities and think tanks, and more exchanges between businesses and industry players. This would lay the groundwork for greater talent mobility and sharing, deeper think-tank exchanges and technological cooperation, and closer integration of regional industrial chains, Huang added. The forum was jointly hosted by the China International Communications Group, Tsinghua University, Xiamen University and Nanyang Technological University, and brought together over 150 representatives from academic institutions, think tanks and media organizations across Asia. Alfred Schipke, director of the East Asian Institute at the National University of Singapore, delivers a keynote speech in the Think Asia Forum 2026 in Singapore, on Nov. 25, 2026. The Think Asia Forum 2026 was held in Singapore on Wednesday, bringing together participants to discuss how openness, innovation and cooperation can drive Asia's development through collaboration in areas such as media, think tanks and local partnerships. (Xinhua/Then Chih Wey)

item.title: Zimbabwe launches China-funded project to combat HIV/AIDS
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 08:37:00
This mobile phone photo taken on Nov. 24, 2026 shows people participating in a launch ceremony of HIV/AIDS response initiatives at Kuwadzana High School in Banket, Zvimba District of Mashonaland West Province, Zimbabwe. (Xinhua/Ye Ting) Zimbabwe on Tuesday launched the Chinese government-funded project on addressing high adolescent girls and young women HIV prevalence in four high-burden provinces, alongside two other initiatives to strengthen the country's HIV/AIDS response. The project was launched at a ceremony held at Kuwadzana High School in Banket, Zvimba District of Mashonaland West Province. Zimbabwean first lady Auxillia Mnangagwa paid tribute to China for its enduring friendship and solidarity with Zimbabwe, noting that the Chinese-funded HIV program reflected the strong bilateral partnership between the two countries and a shared commitment to improving health outcomes and community development in Zimbabwe. "The three initiatives demonstrate our commitment to advancing health development, gender equality and community resilience," she said, also emphasizing the importance of building the capacity of women and girls to respond to climate change so they could enjoy climate-smart livelihoods, as they are often the most affected. Speaking at the same event, Chinese Ambassador to Zimbabwe Zhou Ding said the project, funded by the Chinese government and implemented by UNAIDS Zimbabwe, marked an important milestone in efforts to bolster Zimbabwe's national HIV/AIDS response and to safeguard the health and wellbeing of its most vulnerable communities. This mobile phone photo taken on Nov. 24, 2026 shows Chinese Ambassador to Zimbabwe Zhou Ding speaking at a launch ceremony of HIV/AIDS response initiatives at Kuwadzana High School in Banket, Zvimba District of Mashonaland West Province, Zimbabwe. (Xinhua/Ye Ting) "The project we launch today stands as another powerful demonstration of the deep fraternal bond between China and Zimbabwe. Through our partnership with UNAIDS Zimbabwe, we seek to reinforce Zimbabwe's national efforts to curb HIV transmission, expand equitable access to testing and treatment, and safeguard the health and dignity of thousands of adolescent girls and young women across the four provinces," Zhou said. The project would use comprehensive interventions, including community-based health education, outreach services, wider testing provision and strengthened care referral pathways, to address both the immediate and underlying drivers of HIV transmission and help build healthier, safer and more resilient communities for generations to come, according to Zhou.

item.title: Beijing turns recyclables into public seats, eyeing circular economy
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 08:06:00
A visitor learns about waste plastic recycling process during the 2024 China International Fair for Trade in Services (CIFTIS) at the China National Convention Center in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 14, 2024. (Xinhua/Wu Qinghao) Since the start of the year, Beijing has installed 48 eco-friendly benches made from recycled materials across 26 public spaces, as part of the capital's efforts to promote waste sorting and build a circular economy. The public spaces span historic streets, city parks, waterfront greenways and commercial plazas in seven districts, namely Dongcheng, Xicheng, Chaoyang, Haidian, Fengtai, Shijingshan and Tongzhou, the Beijing Municipal Commission of Urban Management said. The recycled seats come in two main types. The "cloud benches" are made from polypropylene materials such as recycled takeout boxes and plastic drink cups, which go through washing, shredding, modification and injection molding. Each contains material recycled from roughly 1,000 takeout containers. The "board benches" are made from milk cartons that are sorted, stripped of their aluminum and plastic layers, and crushed before being hot-pressed into recycled composite board. Each recycled seat features a sign explaining where its recycled materials came from and how much was used. Beijing has been expanding its recyclables collection system in recent years, linking neighborhood drop-off points, transfer stations and sorting centers so that low-value recyclables such as plastic takeout boxes and drink cups can be collected, transported and processed. This takeout-container recycling network now covers more than 20 universities, parks and railway stations, over 140 office buildings and 11,207 communities with recycling machines. The capital has also launched a citywide online recycling platform that lets residents book door-to-door pickup for old furniture, renovation waste and used appliances, and publishes prices for recyclables such as paper, plastic, metal and textiles. "What matters in building a full recycling chain is not making end products into showpieces, but giving residents feedback when they sort and letting them see the results in public spaces, so that sorting continues to be turned into resources," said Liu Jie, an official with the Beijing Municipal Commission of Urban Management. According to the commission, Beijing will add more recycled benches in more places, including upgraded neighborhoods, improved parks and commercial areas with better walking and cycling routes, while continuing to strengthen its recyclables collection system.

item.title: China and EU avoided the worst outcome, but much more needs to be done: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-26 00:01:00
China EU Photo:VCG This is not the best possible outcome, but it is a pragmatic arrangement that has avoided the worst. The so-called "import quotas" essentially impose restrictions on foreign automakers' exports through compulsory measures. They are inherently protectionist to some extent and, in a broader sense, create uncertainty for the global automotive supply chain. On November 24, the European Commission announced the adoption of import quota restrictions on hybrid vehicles from China and other regions, with the provisional measures set to last for 200 days. China's quota stands at 192,000 vehicles, equivalent to an annual quota of 350,000, higher than that allocated to any other source of imports. On the same day, China's Ministry of Commerce responded by urging Brussels to "earnestly abide by the consensus between the two sides." From the EU's initial proposal to the release of this preliminary ruling, the process involved more than 30 rounds of consultations. The negotiations were arduous, and the outcome was hard-won. This is not the best possible outcome, but it is a pragmatic arrangement that has avoided the worst. The so-called "import quotas" essentially impose restrictions on foreign automakers' exports through compulsory measures. They are inherently protectionist to some extent and, in a broader sense, create uncertainty for the global automotive supply chain. Previously, many voices argued that the introduction of the so-called "import quotas" was specifically aimed at China. This "flawed achievement" represents a pragmatic balance reached by both sides against the broader backdrop of China-EU relations. The EU initially based its calculations on the average import volume over nearly three years, proposing an annual quota of only around 70,000 hybrid vehicles for China, while Japan would have been allocated 257,000 vehicles over the same period. The EU also at one point demanded that China impose so-called "voluntary export restrictions," a request China rejected in accordance with the law and relevant rules. Upholding the three principles of "respect for facts, non-discrimination and compliance with World Trade Organization (WTO) rules," China insisted that the issue be addressed within the framework of the WTO. In the end, China secured a higher quota based on the actual import volume of 302,000 vehicles in 2025. For a provisional measure lasting just 200 days and still at the preliminary ruling stage, the fact that the process did not descend into an escalation of confrontation is already a "second-best solution" under the circumstances. China and the EU are key trading partners to each other, and differences between them are only natural. What is abnormal is treating ordinary industrial competition as a contest over status and resorting to walls and restrictions to ease insecurity. The tortuous consultation process once again demonstrates that, as long as both sides adhere to the principles of mutual respect and equal-footed consultations and address issues within the framework of WTO rules, ways can always be found to manage differences. From the 16 specific point consensus reached at the second meeting of the consultation mechanism in October to the finalization of the latest arrangement on hybrid vehicles, repeated practice has shown that China and the EU have the capacity to transcend differences and achieve mutual benefit and win-win outcomes. Hopefully the EU will earnestly honor the consensus reached by both sides, strictly abide by WTO rules, fully implement the principle of non-discrimination, and conduct relevant investigations in a fair and impartial manner. It is worth noting that trade barriers that should never have existed in the first place reveal Europe's barely concealed industrial anxiety. It is precisely this mounting anxiety that is driving the EU into an increasingly defensive posture, erecting barriers first against battery electric vehicles and then against hybrid vehicles. Faced with the decline of Europe's automotive industry, rather than seeking ways to provide financial support and encourage traditional automakers to innovate and transform, the EU is resorting to tariffs and quotas to buy time for domestic automakers to navigate their transition. Meanwhile, sustained geopolitical engagement and commitments have driven up energy and raw material prices, further increasing the pressure on European automakers to stay afloat. Europe is currently pressing ahead with its green transition in the hope of enhancing its competitiveness, while simultaneously fearing "overdependence" on Chinese green and environmentally friendly products. This reflects a deeply conflicted mindset. In reality, far from driving Europe's traditional automotive industry into a corner as the European side claims, China's new energy vehicles have instead opened up entirely new opportunities. In October this year, German automaker Volkswagen's NEV deliveries in China rose to 4.5 times the level recorded in the same period last year, reaching a record 28,000 units. Deliveries of its ID.AURA T6 model exceeded 12,000 units, making it the best-selling model in the midsize NEV SUV segment. This is a prime example of European automakers proactively integrating into China's industrial and supply chains and achieving market success. Similar success stories abound in other industries. Protectionism offers no way forward; openness and cooperation are the right path. China's recent signing of a protocol with Switzerland to upgrade their free trade agreement and its extension of mutual tariff exemptions with Canada demonstrate the value of dialogue and mutually beneficial cooperation. Europe needs to shake itself out of its self-induced complacency. Hopefully the European side will meet China halfway, provide industries on both sides with a stable, predictable and sustainable environment for trade and investment, and promote the stable, balanced and sound development of bilateral economic and trade relations. China will also closely monitor the progress of the EU's subsequent investigation and reserves all rights, including recourse to dispute settlement and seeking trade compensation under the WTO framework, to resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of the relevant Chinese industries. There is no fundamental conflict of interests between China and Europe, whose industries have complementary strengths and are deeply integrated. A confident, autonomous and open Europe would not only serve the common interests of China and Europe but also enable Europe to find its rightful place amid the sweeping global changes unseen in a century.

item.title: Media coverage of Australia-Solomon security deal full of geopolitical calculations
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 23:21:00
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese (R) speaks during a joint press conference with Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale after signing the Australia-Solomon Islands Treaty at Parliament House in Canberra, Australia, November 25, 2026. Photo: VCG Australia and Solomon Islands signed a security treaty on Wednesday. One day earlier, Australian media had already floated the claim that the Pacific Island Country's (PIC) security pact with China, which will expire in April 2027, is not to be renewed. The way Australian media and other Western media outlets reported the Australia-Solomon pact is worth a closer look. Australia's ABC News, citing a Lowy Institute analyst, described the pact as a "massive win" for Australia. US media such as Politico and British media such as Reuters and the Guardian called it "a blow" for China's ambitions in the Pacific. The asymmetry in vocabulary is itself part of the media "script." Unpack it, and the pattern becomes unmistakable: The words routinely applied to Australia are "partnership," "reassurance," "deepening ties," each of which presupposes legitimacy and reciprocity, while applied to China, the cooperation is encoded as "grip," "foothold," "expansion," each term presupposing erosion and threat. Reading between the lines of such scripts, one cannot help but sense a kind of mean-spirited triumph. When Australia-Solomon cooperation is framed, marketed and celebrated primarily as a means of excluding China, the tell is in the language: The deal is a "massive win" only if someone else has lost; it is newsworthy chiefly as "a blow" to an imaginary rival. The satisfaction that accompanies each "blow" to China and each "win" for Australia is not the satisfaction of a genuine diplomatic achievement, but one of seeing a rival's legitimate presence delegitimized. For a long time, Australia and Western countries have treated China as a hypothetical adversary in the South Pacific. This framing is not incidental - it is the organizing principle behind much of their commentary on the region. When China provides aid and investment to PICs, or engages in normal cooperation with them, these activities are systematically tagged with geopolitical labels. Development assistance is recast as strategic penetration; infrastructure financing is recast as debt leverage; routine diplomatic engagement is recast as interference. The vocabulary shifts, but the function remains the same: to ensure that any Chinese presence in the Pacific is read through the lens of threat rather than through the lens of what it actually delivers. Each claim against China, however thinly sourced, reinforces a broader picture in which China's regional role is inherently illegitimate. The reporting is not aimed at establishing facts; it is aimed at establishing a consensus. And that consensus serves a clear geopolitical agenda: preserving the strategic primacy that Australia and its Western partners have long assumed in the South Pacific. Zhen Feiyang, a research fellow at the Center for Economic Diplomacy, Wuhan University, told the Global Times that since 2025, Australia has accelerated its push for security cooperation arrangements with PICs, including Papua New Guinea, Tonga and Fiji, attempting to build a regional security cooperation network centered on Australia that resembles the US "hub-and-spokes" system in the Asia-Pacific and assertively dominating the regional security order. The cost of this geopolitical agenda, however, is that it locks the entire region into a script of great-power confrontation. Australia and the West could celebrate the "massive win," but what they have lost is the possibility of making the South Pacific a place of genuine cooperation rather than rivalry. Their dream of primacy, too, becomes a casualty - a hegemony that can only be sustained by scripting every Pacific partnership as a contest with China is not a stable order but a permanent state of suspicion, one that exhausts the very influence they seek to preserve. As China stated, "There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and PICs, including Solomon Islands." The statement is a reminder of what the Australian and Western media's script leaves out and why the geopolitical calculations are never really about the Pacific at all.

item.title: GT Voice: India should guard against US attempts to sow discord with China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 22:48:00
India Illustration: Liu Rui/GT The US is again invoking India to advance its own agenda against China. On Tuesday, the Business Standard claimed in a headline: "China leveraging India's supply-chain dependence to curb its rise: US panel." The report cited claims by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission (USCC), which alleged that China is using economic pressure, supply-chain dependencies and its support for Pakistan to constrain India's rise. Dressed up as a warning to India, the USCC report's allegations are in fact an attempt to disguise its deliberate attacks on China as being in India's national interest. It casts China's role in regional supply chains as a threat, portrays mutually beneficial economic ties between China and India as a security risk, and encourages India to view its economic engagement with China through the lens of US strategic competition. But why should India allow its own economic interests to be subordinated to America's strategic agenda? The USCC has a long record of ideological bias against China, leaving its reports with little credibility. Indian readers need not take its allegations too seriously. The question is why the commission is so intent on portraying China as a threat to India's economic development and casting bilateral cooperation in such a negative light. The report itself may offer a clue. In its executive summary, the commission claimed that "Washington and New Delhi have spent a quarter century building closer ties across defense, technology, and trade, but India will continue to guard its strategic autonomy rather than align automatically with US objectives." This may be precisely the problem the commission seeks to address. By portraying China as a threat to India's rise, the report seeks to play up US-China competition and draw India closer to the US position on China. Its allegations about China's intentions toward India should therefore be viewed in light of the commission's strategic agenda and ideological bias against China. There is a more practical way to look at India's economic engagement with China. From April to October, India's exports to China grew by 37.71 percent year-on-year. That figure deserves attention not merely as a measure of export growth, but as a reminder that China is a market offering Indian businesses growing opportunities to expand. Exports have become an important driver of India's economic growth and manufacturing expansion. China is playing an increasingly important part in that story. As India's manufacturing sector develops, the complementarity between the two countries' industrial supply chains is growing, not diminishing. The rise in India's exports to China is one sign of this. Disrupting these mutually beneficial supply-chain links would ultimately come at a cost to India's own economy. The Business Standard report refers repeatedly to China's export controls. This may reflect a concern in Indian public debate. There is, however, a broader context to consider. As China's exports become more technologically advanced and encompass a wider range of dual-use items, applying controls to specific sensitive products in line with established international practice is a normal part of a country's responsibility to uphold international security and meet its nonproliferation obligations. They should not be conflated with restrictions on ordinary trade or mistaken for an obstacle to India's manufacturing development. It is precisely at such times that some Western voices seek to sow discord between the two countries. India has good cause to be alert to such attempts. These voices may have little interest in whether India's economy and manufacturing sector develop smoothly, and may instead be guided by other strategic considerations. India has every reason to assess such arguments with a clear head and make its own judgments. India is right to continue guarding its strategic autonomy rather than aligning automatically with US objectives. The same principle applies to its economic engagement with China. India's trade and industrial interests are for itself to judge, not questions to be settled by the USCC's strategic calculations. A more constructive course is to let China-India economic cooperation grow where it serves both sides.
